PASSAGE 1
That your smartphone is not really yours became clear when Samsung killed its fire-prone
Galaxy Note 7 devices in US with an update in Dec 2016. All connected devices are essentially
services. Russian troops who stole $5mn worth of John Deere tractors from Ukraine in 2022
learnt this the hard way. So, news that RBI might allow lenders to disable financed phones
when EMIs aren’t paid, isn’t alarming technologically. All that needs to be considered are the
ethics of it.

Over the past five years, purchase of phones and white goods on credit has increased
massively – going from 1% in 2020 to 37% last year. Very often, these devices – and phones
especially – are sold to people with poor paying capacity. For lenders, the lure is that sub-
prime borrowers can be charged high rates, but with a high risk of default. So, on their own,
without regulatory clearances, many lenders were installing kill apps on financed phones until
RBI banned the practice last year. However, it’s rethinking its stand now to balance customer
data privacy with lenders’ interests.

The question of data privacy is paramount though. The way these apps have worked so far is
highly invasive. They siphon user data – contacts, photos, messages, location, etc – creating
opportunities for misuse long after a loan has been paid off. In an interview to a website in
2021, the chief of one such app maker said their most effective “nudging” strategy was to
change the wallpaper of a phone – 70% of defaulters paid within a week. But as we’ve seen
with instant loan apps, data in the wrong hands leaves borrowers vulnerable to blackmail. Two
years ago, it was reported that at least 60 Indian borrowers had killed themselves after being
blackmailed with morphed photos, etc.

That’s why strict regulation of apps installed by lenders is crucial. And RBI’s intervention will
hopefully ensure that. The other question – central to RBI’s remit – is the extent of sub-prime
lending itself. Creating an invasive system to protect lenders who are driven by greed to tap
the most unviable customers seems wrong. Perhaps, it’s time for RBI to drill in prudential
norms. ‘Phone’ is a misnomer when your sim is your digital identity, and key to your social
networks and bank accounts. There will be strong temptation to collateralise it for other loans
– home and car loans, for instance – but that idea should be nipped in the bud.

PASSAGE 2
When the new discipline of social psychology was born at the beginning of this century, its
first experiments were essentially adaptations of the suggestion demonstration. The subjects,
usually college students, were asked to give their opinions or preferences concerning various
matters; some time later they were again asked to state their choices, but now they were also
informed of the opinions held by authorities or large groups of their peers on the same matters.
(Often the alleged consensus was fictitious.) Most of these studies had substantially the same
result: Confronted with opinions contrary to their own, many subjects apparently shifted their
judgments in the direction of the view of the majorities or the experts. Other studies reported
that people’s evaluations of the merit of a literary passage could be raised or lowered by
ascribing the passage to different authors. Apparently the sheer weight of numbers or authority
sufficed to change opinions, even when no arguments for the opinions themselves were
provided.

Now, the very ease of success in these experiments arouses suspicion. Did the subjects
actually change their opinions, or were the experimental victories scored only on paper? On
grounds of common sense, one must question whether opinions are generally as watery as
these studies indicate. There is some reason to wonder whether it was not the investigators
who, in their enthusiasm for a theory, were suggestible, and whether the ostensibly gullible
subjects were not providing answers which they thought good subjects were expected to give.

The investigations were guided by the underlying assumptions that people submit uncritically
and painlessly to external manipulation by suggestion or prestige, and that any given idea or
value can be “sold” or “unsold” without reference to its merits. We should be skeptical,
however, of the supposition that the power of social pressure necessarily implies uncritical
submission to it; independence and the capacity to rise above group passion are also open
to human beings. Further, one may question on psychological grounds whether it is possible
to change a person’s judgment of a situation or an object without first changing his or her
knowledge or assumptions about it.

SOURCE: Solomon E. Asch’s essay “Opinions and Social Pressure,”

Donald Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza is far from perfect, but it offers Gazans respite from
the unending violence unleashed by Israel since 2023, and a start towards building the
foundations of lasting peace. Yet, much could still go wrong. To begin with, all principal actors
must agree to the Trump deal. Benjamin Netanyahu has accepted it, though he continues to
oppose Palestinian statehood and has said that Israeli military forces would remain stationed
in most of Gaza. Israel's far-right coalition partners remain opposed. Palestinian Authority (PA)
has called the US president's efforts 'sincere and determined'. But Hamas is yet to issue an
official response. If the group is genuinely committed to a better future for Palestinians, it
should take the deal within the Trump-set deadline.

The peace plan, however, is vague on many fronts. It offers no clarity on the role of Arab and
Muslim states in the redevelopment of Gaza, the training of a police force, or even the
oversight of a 'temporary transitional governance of a technocratic, apolitical Palestinian
committee', nor does it define how PA will be reformed. It recognises the 'aspirations of the
Palestinian people' for statehood but is vague about whether the two-state solution is the


intended goal. Many countries, including India, have welcomed the plan - not because it is
perfect, or because it fulfils Palestinians' right to self-determination and a country of their
own, but because it could finally open the gates for urgently needed humanitarian aid to flow
into Gaza. Once the guns fall silent, it will be up to countries outside the region - such as
India, France and Australia - and regional players like Saudi Arabia and Qatar, to keep the
focus firmly on securing lasting peace for all.

kar nayi parampara ki shuruaat” — which would ostensibly endanger communal amity, and
relocated the banner. But that was not the end of the matter. Over nearly a month since then,
protests against the police action spread across several of Uttar Pradesh’s districts, roiling

disquieting pattern is now ebbing mercifully.

those who criminalised the putting up of an innocuous banner. Indeed, it wasn’t even all that
new, similar banners had been put up in the Kanpur neighbourhood earlier too — in cloth, if
not as a well-lit display board. And what is wrong, anyway, with a “nayi parampara” that does
not disturb the peace? More fundamentally, the question is: In a country where the Constitution
guarantees and protects the right of every citizen to profess and propagate a religion of her

correct this.

A surplus monsoon bodes well for agriculture and rural demand this year. GST reforms, which
kicked in 10 days ago, are also expected to spur consumption. So, RBI’s revised growth
forecast of 6.8% isn’t surprising. It seems like a small increment from 6.5%, but in a $4tn
economy each fraction of a percentage point amounts to billions of dollars. Yet, it’s nothing to
celebrate when Trump’s tariffs have cast a shadow over roughly $50bn worth of goods
exports.

Even otherwise, 6.5% or 6.8% isn’t an aspirational growth rate for India. As the finance ministry
has said more than once this year, India needs to grow at 8% “every year, at least for a
decade” to become a developed country by 2047. Yes, India remains the fastest growing major
economy, but relative performance doesn’t improve living standards. In the late 1990s, when
India’s population was growing at 2% per annum, economists recommended a 9% growth
target for 7% effective growth – to double income every 10 years. Now, although population
growth has slowed to about 1% per year – based on estimates in the absence of a census –
8% is the slowest acceptable GDP growth target. However, a new Morgan Stanley analysis
shows even 8% might be too slow. To address the growing problem of unemployment, the
asking rate must be 12.2%, it says. The report points to record youth unemployment – 17.6%
– and a surge in agricultural employment, which are faces of the same coin. Growing farm
employment is in fact the clearest sign of a jobs crisis. As countries develop, agriculture’s
share in employment and output shrinks. Farm work accounts for only 1.2% of employment in
US. But in India, this year’s Economic Survey showed agriculture’s share in employment
increased from 44.1% in 2017-18 to 46.1% in 2023-24.

Over the next 10 years, 84mn Indians – equal to the population of Germany – will hit working
age. So, creating good jobs for them has to be a national priority. Long-neglected
manufacturing, whose share in GDP had slipped to 15.9% in 2023-24 from 16.7% in 2013-14,
should be the preferred engine for this, because it creates more related jobs than services.
That’s how US built its middle class in the 1950s, and China in the 2000s. The vision of
developed India hinges on this.

questions.stimulus:
PASAGE 10
The right to freedom under Articles 19–22 of the Indian Constitution forms the core of the
democratic project: it mediates the relationship between the individual and the State by
recognising liberties that enable participation, dissent, and self-expression. Yet these
freedoms are not absolute. Article 19(1) guarantees rights such as speech, assembly,
movement, residence, and profession, while Article 19(2)–(6) authorise “reasonable
restrictions” in the interests of security, public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, or to
ensure professional regulation and social welfare. The tension between liberty and regulation
is therefore structural, not exceptional. Courts routinely emphasise that restrictions must be
narrowly tailored: they must be proximate to a legitimate aim, proportionate in effect, and non-
arbitrary in application. Mere administrative discomfort or political disagreement cannot justify


curbing fundamental freedoms. The nature of restrictions varies across rights. Free speech is
particularly vulnerable to overbroad limitations justified in the name of public order. Courts
have resisted such expansions, holding that hypothetical or remote threats cannot qualify as
“reasonable restrictions.” Peaceful assemblies, too, may be regulated but not suppressed
outright; blanket prohibitions fail the test of proportionality unless accompanied by
demonstrable, imminent risks. Freedom of movement and residence is more often regulated
through statutory schemes relating to public health, criminal procedure, or national security,
but even these restrictions must meet the test of procedural fairness and necessity. The right
to life and personal liberty under Article 21 interacts closely with the freedom rights. Preventive
detention laws, for instance, are constitutionally permitted but tightly circumscribed by
procedural safeguards; courts insist that detention cannot be based on stale materials or
vague apprehensions. Similarly, custodial rights, such as the right to counsel and protection
against arbitrary arrest, serve as practical guarantees of personal liberty. Article 22 attempts
to strike a balance by allowing preventive detention while mandating disclosure of grounds,
representation before advisory boards, and time limits. Emerging debates further complicate
the landscape. Digital speech, algorithmic policing, and virtual assemblies raise questions
about whether traditional tests of “public order” or “reasonableness” remain adequate.
Scholars argue that excessive algorithmic surveillance chills freedom even without explicit
prohibitions. Ultimately, the right to freedom is best understood not as a static list of
entitlements but as an evolving equilibrium between individual autonomy and democratic
governancean equilibrium courts must continually renegotiate in light of changing
technologies, social conflicts, and state imperatives.

PASAGE 11
The distinction between an employee and an independent contractor remains one of the most
litigated questions in Indian labour jurisprudence. Although no single statute lays down an
exhaustive test, courts have evolved a combination of indicators: the control and supervision
test, the integration test, the economic dependence test, and, in modern settings, the
entrepreneurial/“multiple clients” test. Traditionally, the dominant factor was the employer’s
right to direct how, when, and where work must be done. A worker subject to detailed
instructions, mandatory office hours, and disciplinary oversight was more likely to be classified
as an employee. However, courts increasingly emphasise the substance of the relationship
rather than contractual labels. Merely calling someone a “consultant” or “freelancer” is
irrelevant if the actual working conditions reflect subordination. The rise of platform work, gig
services, and outsourced operations complicates this determination. A delivery rider may use
her own vehicle and enjoy flexible hours yet remain economically dependent on one platform,
subjected to algorithmic ratings and unilateral termination factors pointing toward employee-
like vulnerability. Conversely, a software architect who works project-to-project for several
clients, bears financial risk, and negotiates deliverables independently is more likely to be
treated as a contractor. Courts also consider who supplies tools, whether tax/PF deductions


are made, and whether the worker can delegate tasks to others. Misclassification carries
consequences. If a purported contractor is found to be an employee, the principal may owe
statutory benefits such as provident fund, gratuity, maternity benefits, and compliance with
working-hour norms. On the other hand, contractors normally receive only contractual
remedies unless the contract is unconscionable. The challenge lies in blended arrangements:
hybrid teams, remote-gig models, and “zero-hour” engagements where indicia point in
different directions. Indian courts adopt a “composite test,” weighing factors cumulatively. No
single factor is dispositive; the ultimate question is whether the worker is in a relationship of
subordination and economic dependence. Where evidence is evenly balanced, courts typically
tilt toward recognising employee status, emphasising labour-protective principles. The
jurisprudence thus reflects a tension between commercial flexibility and the need to prevent
disguised employment structures designed to evade welfare obligations.

PASAGE 12
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India operates at the intersection of environmental
governance, administrative duty, and public accountability. Under the Environment Protection
Act, 1986, large-scale industries, infrastructure projects, mining operations, and certain
categories of manufacturing units must undergo an EIA before commencing operations. The
purpose of the EIA is not to halt development, but to ensure that development proceeds with
awareness of its ecological costs. At its core, an EIA requires the project proponent to identify
potential environmental impacts, propose mitigation strategies, and subject the proposal to
independent appraisal by an Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC). The process typically
involves four elements: screening (to determine if an EIA is required), scoping (to define the
extent of study), public consultation (where affected communities express concerns), and
appraisal (where the EAC evaluates whether the project should be granted environmental
clearance). Not all projects require a full EIA; certain activities fall under exempted categories
or are subject only to preliminary scrutiny. Even where required, the clearance is not a one-
time permission; the law envisages post-clearance monitoring, compliance reporting, and
possible suspension for violations. Recent disputes reveal recurring problems. Some project
proponents treat EIA as a procedural formality: copying baseline data, ignoring cumulative
impacts, or restricting public hearings. Others argue that delays and excessive compliance
discourage investment. Courts have held that EIA is a substantive safeguard: the duty to
assess impacts is not satisfied by filing volumes of documents, but by demonstrating genuine
environmental due diligence. A clearance obtained by concealing crucial information or
bypassing public consultation may be struck down, even after substantial investment.
Ambiguities remain, especially regarding “expansion projects,” where existing industries seek
to increase capacity. Authorities must decide whether expansions trigger fresh EIAs or only
require amendment of existing clearances. Another grey area concerns the legal status of
draft EIAs; though not final, they must still accurately disclose material facts. Ultimately, the
EIA regime is designed to balance ease of doing business with the constitutional imperative
of environmental protection. It expects accuracy, transparency, and proactive environmental
stewardshipnot mechanical compliance.

PASAGE 13
 For decades, India's labour laws were a labyrinth of over 29 central enactments, creating
confusion for employers and loopholes for exploitation. In a historic overhaul, Parliament
consolidated these into four comprehensive Labour Codes: the Code on Wages, the Code on
Social Security, the Industrial Relations Code, and the Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code. This shift aims to balance the ease of doing business with the
protection of workers' rights in a modern economy. A pivotal change is the universalisation of
minimum wages. Previously restricted to "scheduled employments," the Code on Wages now
mandates that no employee across any sector can be paid less than the statutory minimum
wage. This creates a non-negotiable floor for income. Simultaneously, the Code on Social
Security expands the safety net beyond the traditional factory floor. It explicitly recognises "gig
workers" and "platform workers" like food delivery agents and ride-sharing drivers, granting
them access to social security schemes for the first time. This acknowledges the reality of the
gig economy, where the employer-employee relationship is often blurred. The Industrial
Relations Code introduces a significant restructuring of disputes and strikes. It mandates a
14-day notice period for strikes in all industrial establishments, not just public utility services.
This is designed to encourage dialogue and prevent abrupt work stoppages. Furthermore, it
raises the threshold for "standing orders" (rules of conduct for workmen) to apply only to
establishments with 300 or more workers, giving smaller businesses more flexibility in hiring
and firing, a move that critics argue creates a "hire and fire" regime. Finally, the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code streamlines safety regulations. It introduces a
single license for staffing firms and allows women to work night shifts (7 PM to 6 AM) in all
establishments, provided their consent is obtained and adequate safety measures are in
place. This provision attempts to remove legal barriers to women's employment while placing
a positive duty on the employer to ensure their safety. The overarching legal principle binding
these codes is the movement from rigid, sector-specific rules to broader, universally applicable
standards that recognise new forms of employment while attempting to streamline compliance
for industries.

     through a mobile app. The workers choose their own hours and use their own tools.
     QuickReach argues it is merely a technology aggregator and not an employer, hence it
     has no obligation to provide any benefits to these workers. Based on the passage, which
     of the following is the most logical legal outcome under the new framework?

options.label: a
options.text:
QuickReach is exempt because freelance workers are independent contractors and do
not fall under the definition of "employee" in any labour code.

options.label: b
options.text:
QuickReach will be required to provide access to social security schemes, as the new
Code explicitly recognizes "gig and platform workers" and extends benefits to them despite
the blurred employer-employee relationship.

options.label: c
options.text:
QuickReach is liable to pay minimum wages but not social security, as the Code on
Wages applies to all sectors, but social security is restricted to factory workers.

options.label: d
options.text:
QuickReach is exempt because the Code on Social Security only applies to traditional
industries with fixed working hours.

questions.stimulus:
PASAGE 13
 For decades, India's labour laws were a labyrinth of over 29 central enactments, creating
confusion for employers and loopholes for exploitation. In a historic overhaul, Parliament
consolidated these into four comprehensive Labour Codes: the Code on Wages, the Code on
Social Security, the Industrial Relations Code, and the Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code. This shift aims to balance the ease of doing business with the
protection of workers' rights in a modern economy. A pivotal change is the universalisation of
minimum wages. Previously restricted to "scheduled employments," the Code on Wages now
mandates that no employee across any sector can be paid less than the statutory minimum
wage. This creates a non-negotiable floor for income. Simultaneously, the Code on Social
Security expands the safety net beyond the traditional factory floor. It explicitly recognises "gig
workers" and "platform workers" like food delivery agents and ride-sharing drivers, granting
them access to social security schemes for the first time. This acknowledges the reality of the
gig economy, where the employer-employee relationship is often blurred. The Industrial
Relations Code introduces a significant restructuring of disputes and strikes. It mandates a
14-day notice period for strikes in all industrial establishments, not just public utility services.
This is designed to encourage dialogue and prevent abrupt work stoppages. Furthermore, it
raises the threshold for "standing orders" (rules of conduct for workmen) to apply only to
establishments with 300 or more workers, giving smaller businesses more flexibility in hiring
and firing, a move that critics argue creates a "hire and fire" regime. Finally, the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code streamlines safety regulations. It introduces a
single license for staffing firms and allows women to work night shifts (7 PM to 6 AM) in all
establishments, provided their consent is obtained and adequate safety measures are in
place. This provision attempts to remove legal barriers to women's employment while placing
a positive duty on the employer to ensure their safety. The overarching legal principle binding
these codes is the movement from rigid, sector-specific rules to broader, universally applicable
standards that recognise new forms of employment while attempting to streamline compliance
for industries.

https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2025/11/29/india-four-labour-codes-overview-
explained-scctimes/, 29-11-2025
questions.stem:
The workers of a private automobile manufacturing unit, "AutoCorp," are unhappy with
      a new shift policy. Without any prior warning, the union announces an immediate strike
      starting the next morning to paralyze production and force the management to
      negotiate. Under the Industrial Relations Code described in the passage, is this strike
      legal?

options.text:
Yes, because private manufacturing units are not "public utility services," and therefore,
workers retain the right to strike immediately to protect their interests.

options.label: b
options.text:
No, because the new Code mandates a 14-day notice period for strikes in all industrial
establishments to encourage dialogue and prevent abrupt stoppages.

options.label: c
options.text:
Yes, provided the union represents more than 50% of the workforce, the strike is a valid
method of collective bargaining.

options.label: d
options.text:
No, because strikes are now completely banned in the manufacturing sector to promote
the "ease of doing business."

       engineer, which would require her to work from 8 PM to 4 AM. Ms. Rao is willing to take

questions.stimulus:
PASAGE 14
 India’s digital ecosystem is dominated by a few large platforms, especially in messaging and
social media. A key problem is platform lock-in: when users are unable to switch services or
communicate across apps because one platform holds most of the network. For instance,
when WhatsApp became massively used, competing apps like Hike Messenger and Arattai
found it almost impossible to gain traction. Platform interoperability, where different apps can
communicate seamlessly, offers a solution. Interoperability means that a user on one
messenger can send messages to a user on another, even if they are on different apps. Legal
analysts argue that India is now at a crossroads: traditionally, competition law focused on data
protection, privacy and dominance; but in the platform era there is also a need for
interoperability regulation. Proponents point to fintech and telecom examples: the Unified
Payments Interface (UPI) created interoperable payments across different apps and broke the
wallet-lock-in. Similarly, mobile number portability allowed telecom users to switch providers
easily. These experiences suggest that messaging and social-media interoperability are
feasible. Critics caution that forcing interoperability might dilute privacy or security standards
or impose heavy burdens on smaller apps. In India, the regulation of social media and
messaging apps is still evolving. Industry observers stress that regulating interoperability
requires protecting encryption, ensuring fair competition, safeguarding user choice, and
preventing winner-take-all dominance. If large platforms are required to allow interoperability,
new entrants may compete on features, quality, service not users locked into a network. The
discussion is thus not only technical, but fundamentally about user freedom, competition, and
regulation in the digital age.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.livelaw.in/articles/zoho-arattai-platform-
interoperability-and-social-media-regulation-311643, 29-11-2025

questions.stimulus:
PASAGE 15
 The Competition Commission of India’s (CCI) recent investigation into Apple’s App Store
practices has triggered a constitutional challenge that raises deeper questions about the
structure of antitrust penalties in India. The probe began after complaints alleging that Apple’s
mandatory in-app payment system and commission of up to 30% unfairly restricted
competition by raising costs for developers and forcing them to use Apple’s proprietary billing
mechanism. In 2024, the CCI’s investigation unit concluded that Apple had abused its
dominant position, describing the App Store as an “unavoidable trading partner” for developers
seeking to reach iOS users. The dispute escalated after Parliament amended Section 27(b)
of the Competition Act in 2023. Earlier, penalties could be based only on “relevant turnover,”
meaning turnover linked to the offending product or service. Following the amendment,
“turnover” is now interpreted as global turnover derived from all products and services. In
2024, the CCI’s Monetary Penalty Guidelines reinforced this shift by allowing the regulator to
rely on global turnover, especially when determining “relevant turnover” is infeasible, and to
increase penalties if necessary for deterrence. Apple contends that this regime is
unconstitutional, disproportionate, and arbitrary. It argues that penalties must be connected to


the scale of the violation within India, not tied to unrelated global revenue streams. To
demonstrate alleged absurdity, Apple analogised its situation to punishing a toy-and-stationery
seller’s entire ₹20,000 turnover for a violation limited to ₹100 worth of toys. Apple further
claims the amendment may be applied retrospectively, pointing to a recent CCI decision where
new rules were used for violations committed a decade earlier. The CCI, however, maintains
that global turnover penalties align with practices in jurisdictions such as the European Union,
where fines of up to 10% of global turnover are standard, especially for large digital platforms
whose market power extends beyond territorial borders. The underlying policy shift reflects
concerns that penalties based solely on Indian revenue may be too small to deter multinational
tech giants. The Delhi High Court must now decide whether Parliament’s decision to adopt a
global-turnover framework strikes a constitutionally acceptable balance between regulatory
deterrence and proportional punishment, or whether it impermissibly overreaches by linking
Indian violations to worldwide financial metrics.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://indianexpress.com/article/technology/tech-
reviews/apple-14-inch-macbook-pro-m5-silicon-review-10393983/?ref=infinite, 30-11-2025

fats. Now, the argumentative Indian would insist that pan India’s basic rice-atta/maida staple

ever-increasing physical inactivity. And it’s not as simple as just replacing ‘bad’ carbs with
fancy organics.

decreasing overall carbohydrate quantity doesn’t reduce risk of T2D or abdominal obesity.
The survey found that risk of T2D or prediabetes can be reduced by 6-10% if carbs are
replaced with fish or egg – but meat does not have the same impact. Also, barring Jharkhand,

The publication of Bihar’s final voter list after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), begun in
June, dispels anxieties on both sides of the political spectrum. Fears of large-scale voter
disenfranchisement, raised by the Opposition and civil society, proved unfounded: the list
stands at 7.42 crore, only 6% lower than June’s 7.89 crore. This result owes much to the
pressure applied by the Opposition, the Supreme Court’s oversight, and vigilant media
reporting. Meanwhile, the SIR’s other declared aim—to remove “illegal immigrants” or
“ghuspaithiya” from the rolls—did not produce significant evidence of such infiltration. The
SIR’s unprecedentedly strict requirements placed the burden of proving citizenship on voters,
converting the updating of rolls into a citizenship test, especially hard for undocumented and
marginalised people. Ultimately, 68.6 lakh names were deleted, mostly for death, migration,
or duplication, with only a negligible number of foreigners found, undermining claims of
widespread electoral manipulation by outsiders.
Supreme Court interventions prompted key modifications to the SIR in response to legal
challenges over its timing and intent, as well as Opposition and media scrutiny. The Court
insisted on greater transparency in voter deletions, stated reasons, and inclusion of Aadhaar
as a valid document. This experience demonstrates the value of checks and balances in a
constitutional democracy. Going forward, as the EC extends SIR to other states, it must ensure
inclusivity, considering the diverse realities of different contexts. Routine electoral roll
cleanups are essential, and intensive revisions—including house-to-house enumerations—
are sometimes necessary to reflect urbanisation, migration, and demographic change.
The Bihar SIR, however, also highlighted moments where the Election Commission appeared
partial, sometimes behaving more as a political actor than a neutral body. In future, the EC
must strive for greater equanimity and humility, restoring faith in its impartiality and fairness.
The Bihar SIR experience should serve as a guide for the Commission to reaffirm its legacy
of independence, neutrality, and trustworthiness.

26. This is higher than RBI’s 6.5% projection made in August. It has also revised its inflation
forecast for the current fiscal year downward from 3.1% in August to 2.6% now. This is the
lowest-ever inflation rate, within the RBI's 2%-6% target band, since the current series began
in 2012-13. And a 6.8% growth rate is above India’s potential growth rate. These numbers
paint a perfect picture for the macro economy that is doing good in terms of growth without
triggering inflation. Is the Indian economy in the so-called Goldilocks state, where it is neither
too hot nor too cold? There is good reason to exercise some caution in jumping to this
conclusion.

than-expected inflation, not stronger economic momentum. As a result, the nominal growth

further changes. The Indian economy isn’t in as sweet a spot as the latest growth and inflation
projections suggest it is — but there is nothing that suggests a deep-rooted crisis as well, and
this is exactly why the MPC’s pause is a prudent one.

PASSAGE 19
Demographers at the United Nations predict that the number of humans on Earth will begin
shrinking as soon as 2080 — the culmination of a global decline in birthrates that began two
generations ago. I keep thinking about what this shift means for moms. Fewer women are
having children. Those who do are having smaller families than previous generations. This
trend transcends the norms of any one culture or place. The shift away from motherhood is
happening slowly — but surely. It’s a source of growing bipartisan concern. New Pew
Research polling finds that over half of Americans (53%) now say fewer people choosing to
have children in the future would negatively impact the United States, a six-point increase from
last year. There have been other times and places of falling fertility due to famine, plague or
war. But this depopulation is unique in the experience of humanity because (1) it appears to
be what we are self-selecting into, and (2) it’s worldwide.

It can be argued that to the extent this shift better reflects preferences and choice, it’s a good
thing. I, for one, am relieved to have three children, not twelve. But politicians and academics
are worried about the sociodemographic implications. After all, birthrates below replacement
eventually result in human extinction. We don’t know how this will play out over the long run.
Maybe a world with fewer children means a greater level of investment in each of them. Or
maybe it shrinks the share of the population interested in helping kids. Maybe technology
alleviates any shortages in the workforce or the taxpayer base. But I can’t help thinking about
how this will turn up the anxiety American moms already are feeling. Because declining
birthrates not only mean fewer babies — declining birthrates also mean fewer moms.

There’s also more pressure on parents to keep children entertained. Children are not around
other children as much socially as they used to be; even within families, there are fewer
siblings. So kids look to mom and dad for playtime — or to screens. I think about all of the
anxiety on mothers’ shoulders about whether they are feeding their kids the right things,
whether their school is teaching children what they need to know, the significant financial
investment in college, and how much that this pressure to “do parenting right” will only increase
if you only have one or maybe two children.


SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-10-04/birth-rates-are-falling-can-
the-world-handle-fewer-moms

questions.stimulus:
Direction (111-116): Study the following information carefully and answer the
      questions given below.
      Digital literacy plays a critical role in socio-economic development, enabling access to
      education, financial services, and governance. In India, however, a significant disparity
      exists in the extent and nature of internet access and digital skills between urban and
      rural populations. While urban populations generally have better access to high-speed
      broadband, subsidized connectivity schemes, and higher levels of digital competence,
      rural populations face challenges such as limited network infrastructure, high device
      costs, and lower awareness about digital services. This urban-rural divide in digital
      adoption highlights the broader issue of digital inequality, making it essential to analyse
      the factors contributing to this gap and explore strategies for more inclusive digital
      protection. A nationwide digital access survey was conducted.
      The survey covered 1,20,000 adults across urban and rural areas. Urban residents
      formed 60% of the sample (that is, 72,000 people) while rural residents made up 40%
      (that is, 48,000 people). In each area, digital status was classified under four heads –
      Daily Internet Users, Infrequent Users, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet), and
      Digitally Excluded.
      In urban areas, Daily Internet Users accounted for 45% of the urban population,
      Infrequent Users for 25%, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet) for 10%, and the
      remaining 20% were Digitally Excluded. In rural areas, where digital access is generally
      lower, Daily Internet Users stood at 15%, Infrequent Users at 15%, Basic Smartphone
      Users (no internet) at 25%, while 45% were Digitally Excluded. For this survey,
      "Digitally Enabled" includes everyone who uses the internet (Daily + Infrequent users),
      and "Digitally Excluded" indicates those with no regular digital engagement (Basic
      Smartphone + Excluded).

What is the total number of people in the
